This is a large task, so I'm planning a thorough JUnit 4 test suite for NodeUtil, placing it in the same package since many methods are package-private, and covering key methods with boundary, null, and malformed input cases using IR builder methods to construct nodes.

I'm listing out the full set of methods to cover, including boolean/string/number value extraction, operator classification (symmetric, relational, associative, commutative, assignment), side-effect analysis (mutable state, function calls, constructors), local result checks, immutability, precedence, and utility predicates like isGet and referencesThis, to make sure the test suite has broad coverage.

Continuing to expand the list, I'm covering control-flow related helpers (loops, control structures, switch cases, try/catch/finally), function-related checks (declarations, expressions, hoisting, var-args, bleeding names), assignment/lvalue detection, object literal key handling, operator string conversion, qualified name construction and validation, and variable declaration extraction — rounding out the full scope of NodeUtil functionality that needs test coverage.

Given the sheer number of methods, I'll narrow down to a representative but branch-rich subset rather than attempting exhaustive coverage of every single method, since full coverage isn't feasible in reasonable time.

I need to figure out how to construct a CodingConvention instance for tests involving qualified name nodes -- checking whether there's a default implementation like GoogleCodingConvention or ClosureCodingConvention available in this codebase.

Since the CodingConvention interface isn't visible in the source, I should avoid guessing its behavior. I'll skip tests for newQualifiedNameNode variants, isConstantByConvention, and the AbstractCompiler-dependent overloads of mayEffectMutableState and functionCallHasSideEffects to prevent unfounded assumptions.

For building test node trees, I'll rely on the IR builder class from com.google.javascript.rhino, using its various static factory methods for constructing nodes representing literals, control flow, expressions, and functions.

Given this is an older Closure-compiler version predating IR helpers, I'll build nodes manually using direct Node constructors with Token types, plus addChildToBack/addChildrenToBack for assembling children, and Node.newString/Node.newNumber for literals.

Using addChildToBack to build multi-child nodes like the HOOK ternary is safer than relying on multi-arg constructors, so I'll apply that pattern consistently. I'm fairly confident basic factory methods and getter methods like getDouble/getString exist on Node since NodeUtil source relies on them, though I'm double-checking whether a simple public Node(int type) constructor is actually available.

But then I realize Node lives in a different package than the test class, so any package-private or protected constructors won't be accessible - this is a real risk since Rhino-style Node classes often restrict direct construction and expect external code to go through the IR facade or public static factories like Node.newString/newNumber instead.

This actually confirms IR is the intended public API for jscomp code to create nodes, since NodeUtil itself imports and calls IR methods like IR.exprResult(). I need to recall the exact structure of Closure Compiler's real IR.java as closely as I can.

Continuing to trace IR method signatures... IR.name(String) makes NAME nodes, IR.thisNode() makes THIS, IR.string(String) makes STRING, IR.getprop takes two Node args, and IR.var has both single-arg and two-arg (name, initializer) forms.

I'm also confirming other constructors: assign takes two Nodes, voidNode wraps a Node, number takes a double, trueNode/falseNode take no args, neg wraps a Node, and call takes a single target Node with additional arguments appended via addChildToBack.

This confirms that addChildToBack is called from the jscomp package, meaning it's a public Node method alongside getFirstChild, getNext, getType, getString, getDouble, and srcref. So once I have a Node instance, I can manipulate its children directly through these accessible methods rather than relying on IR for every operation.

Since NodeUtil never calls `new Node(...)` directly and always uses IR instead, I should stick with IR plus these confirmed public instance methods rather than assuming the constructor is accessible. I'll limit myself to the IR factory methods explicitly shown in the source (exprResult, block, empty, var with one or two arguments) combined with well-established Closure compiler conventions I'm confident about.

Given the risk of getting exact overloads wrong for things like TRY, CATCH, LABEL, and STRING_KEY, I think the safest approach is to stick only with IR methods I'm fully confident about—the ones confirmed from source or that are extremely standard—and find workarounds for anything less certain.

For node types without simple factories, like FUNCTION, WHILE, IF, TRY, NEW, or PARAM_LIST, I'm wondering if I can construct them and then modify the type afterward, but that seems risky since I'm not sure a public setType exists. A more promising alternative might be Rhino's own legacy Node static factories, like Node.newString(int type, String str), which historically have been public and widely used.

Given the age of this Closure defect and the likelihood these legacy factories still exist for backward compatibility, I'll settle on using IR only for confirmed methods, and fall back to a helper that constructs nodes directly via `new Node(type)` for everything else, flagging that as an assumption I need to verify.

Since this is Defects4J Closure-174, the actual full source tree—including IR.java, Node.java, and Token.java—exists on the classpath, so I can reasonably write against the real API rather than inventing behavior not present in the source.

For for-in loops, I recall that structure needs a 3-child FOR node (item, obj, body) rather than the standard 4-child version, so I might need a different constructor like IR.forIn, though I'm not certain of the exact name. Given my uncertainty, I'll just pick a reasonable choice and flag it with a comment.

Given the moderate effort level, I'll aim for a solid but not exhaustive test class, covering a good portion of branches with reasonably safe API usage and clear comments where I'm making assumptions. I'll organize tests into logical groups with helper factory methods for common node patterns like names, numbers, and strings, then write out roughly 50-60 test methods.

I'll be selective and avoid risky constructs like FOR-IN or TRY/CATCH that require uncertain API structures, focusing instead on well-understood utility functions like getStringValue, getPureBooleanValue, isImmutableValue, isSymmetricOperation, getInverseOperator, and operator-related helpers.

I should also cover functions related to precedence, undefined/null checks, associativity and commutativity, naming validity (simple, qualified, property names), literal value checks, and array/string extraction helpers, along with assignment and loop structure detection where feasible.

Continuing through more utility checks: control structure and loop code block extraction, condition expressions, statement blocks, switch cases, reference names, call/new target detection, and side effect analysis for function calls, constructors, and general nodes -- plus function expression/declaration detection which needs a parent context, so I'll attach nodes to a BLOCK/SCRIPT for testing purposes.

Continuing through more helpers...

Wrapping the function node inside a block lets me confirm it registers as a statement, since isFunctionDeclaration relies on the parent being SCRIPT/BLOCK/LABEL. For a function expression instead, I just need to attach it as a child of an assignment or call rather than a statement block.

Actually, the cleanest fix is to just directly attach the function node as a child to an ARRAYLIT node using addChildToBack, sidestepping IR wrapper validation concerns entirely.

For an expression context, I can build an empty ARRAYLIT and add the function as a child so its parent isn't a statement container. For a statement context, I can build an empty BLOCK and add the function so its parent naturally makes it recognized as a statement.

I'm cataloguing which IR factory methods are safe to call with no or minimal arguments—things like block(), empty(), trueNode(), falseNode(), nullNode(), thisNode(), name(String), string(String), number(double), paramList(), arraylit(), and objectlit()—so I can rely on manual addChildToBack calls instead of validated varargs constructors.

But nodes like NOT, AND, OR, HOOK, ASSIGN, GETPROP, CALL, VAR, IF, FUNCTION, and similar require at least one child argument at construction time, meaning any internal Preconditions checks (like requiring a NAME node for a var's lhs) would fire immediately rather than letting me build an empty shell first.

That risk is mitigated by choosing sensible node types matching real semantic usage, so runtime validation should generally pass — the real risk is just getting exact method names, arity, and parameter types right for compilation. I'll trust my recollection of Closure Compiler's IR class and commit to it, using IR.string and IR.number for literal construction rather than Node's static methods directly.

For regexp nodes I'll construct them from a string pattern node, and I'll skip GETTER_DEF/SETTER_DEF entirely since I'm unsure of their factory methods — testing isGetOrSetKey with a plain STRING or NAME node instead to avoid that risk.

For STRING_KEY nodes, I'm confident `IR.stringKey(String, Node)` exists for object literal keys, so I'll construct one like `IR.stringKey("foo", IR.number(1))` to test the object-lit-key-related functions.

GETPROP requires the property to be a STRING node, matching the source's usage pattern. For NEW nodes, I recall the method is likely named `IR.newNode` since 'new' is reserved, and CALL nodes take a target plus variadic args similarly.

FUNCTION nodes need a NAME node (possibly anonymous), a param list, and a body block. IF nodes have 2-arg and 3-arg (with else) forms, useful for condition-related utilities, though I'm less confident about TRY, CATCH, and LABEL node helpers, so I'll limit their use.

Given the precise child-ordering requirements for TRY nodes (try block, catch-container, optional finally block) and uncertainty about the exact factory method names, I'll skip testing the TRY/CATCH/LABEL-related methods to avoid getting the structure wrong.

For loops, I'm more confident about the standard factory methods for WHILE, DO, and FOR nodes, so I'll go ahead and test isLoopStructure, getLoopCodeBlock, and isControlStructureCodeBlock using those. Now I'm thinking through FOR-IN handling and the isForIn check.

Since I can't confidently construct a for-in node with the right child structure, I'll skip testing the true branch and instead cover the false case using a WHILE node, adding a note about the missing constructor confidence. I'll also skip LABEL entirely and reconsider which control structure node types I can safely test given the constructors I'm avoiding.

I need to check whether the default branch of isControlStructureCodeBlock actually throws an exception rather than returning false when given an unhandled control structure type, since that changes how I need to test it.

So testing the default branch means expecting an IllegalStateException, which I can trigger by passing a parent that isn't a control structure type at all (like a NAME node) — a simple test case without complex node construction. I'll add that test, then move on to verifying isControlStructure itself with a few straightforward true cases.

For the true-return checks, I need actual Node instances of each control structure type (IF, FOR, WHILE, DO, TRY, SWITCH, CASE, DEFAULT_CASE, LABEL, CATCH, WITH), but I only have confirmed IR helper methods for IF/WHILE/DO/FOR — the rest would require constructing nodes directly by type constant since there's no dedicated builder for them.

Actually, recalling more carefully, Rhino's Node class likely kept public constructors since so much AST code across the codebase constructs nodes directly with `new Node(Token.XXX)`, and Closure's fork probably preserved that same public API for compatibility.

I now recall Node constructors are indeed public and widely used directly across the Closure Compiler codebase, which simplifies things considerably. I'll build nodes using the public constructors with Token constants directly, plus helper methods like addChildToBack and addChildrenToBack.

For string, number, and name nodes I'll use the static factory methods Node.newNumber and Node.newString, which cover the common IR construction cases including NAME nodes. I'll also rely on the standard child-navigation getters like getFirstChild, getLastChild, getNext, getChildCount, and hasChildren alongside the addChild methods.

I'm also noting the boolean type-check helpers (isName, isBlock, isFunction, etc.) and accessor methods like getParent, getString, getDouble, and getType, since NodeUtil's own source relies on these directly, confirming they're safe to use.

For building nodes with specific structures, I need addChildToBack, which NodeUtil.newCallNode also demonstrates as accessible, plus the Node constructors that take a type alone, a type with one child, or a type with two children.

Writing node-building helper...

This gives full flexibility to build any node type—FUNCTION, FOR, TRY, CATCH, LABEL, SWITCH, CASE, WITH, REGEXP, PARAM_LIST, and more—using addChildToBack for structure and Node.newString/newNumber for leaf values like NAME, STRING, and NUMBER. I'll commit fully to this approach and avoid the IR class entirely to minimize API assumptions.

I want to verify one risk though: whether the public `Node(int type)` constructor actually exists in Closure-174's Node class, and I'm recalling that the real implementation does set type, parent, and sourcePosition in exactly that way.

Beyond that base constructor, I'm also confident there are public multi-argument overloads for one, two, three, or an array of children, plus a lineno/charno variant — matching familiar patterns from this codebase. I'll proceed using both the simple constructor-plus-addChildToBack approach and the direct multi-child constructors where convenient, like building a ternary HOOK node directly from its three parts.

I'll also rely on the newString and newNumber helper factory methods, and I'll reference Token constants directly along with TernaryValue for checking boolean-value assertions.

Now I'm setting up the test file's package declaration and imports for JUnit assertions plus the relevant Node, Token, and jstype classes.

Building small helper methods to construct Node instances for names, strings, and numbers, then planning to write a large, systematic set of test methods covering the various IR utility methods one by one.

I'm working through boolean value logic tests now — checking ASSIGN, COMMA, NOT, AND, and OR node combinations against expected pure boolean outcomes like TRUE and FALSE.

For getPureBooleanValue, I'm testing HOOK expressions with matching vs. differing branches (TRUE vs UNKNOWN), plus array/object literals as always TRUE, VOID as FALSE, and primitives like strings, numbers, and null against their truthy/falsy equivalents.

I'm continuing to trace edge cases: VOID nodes without side effects resolve FALSE, but wrapping a call to an unrecognized function inside VOID triggers side-effect detection and forces UNKNOWN. I'm also checking special NAME tokens like "undefined", "NaN", "Infinity", and generic identifiers, plus confirming TRUE and REGEXP literals evaluate to TRUE.

Now I'm examining ARRAYLIT nodes—empty array literals have no side effects and resolve TRUE, but arrays containing calls to unknown functions would trigger side-effect detection instead.

OBJECTLIT should behave the same way. For the default fall-through case in getPureBooleanValue, something like an ADD node with two number operands wouldn't match any explicit case label, so it drops straight through to UNKNOWN at the bottom—that's a good test case to verify the default path.

Now shifting to getStringValue: STRING nodes just return their string, and I want to test STRING_KEY too, constructing it with newString since it likely stores its name the same way NAME nodes do, so getString() should return "key". For NAME nodes, "undefined", "Infinity", and "NaN" return their name directly, but a plain NAME like "x" won't match those checks, breaks out of the switch, and falls through to return null at the end—that's another useful case to verify.

Continuing through the cases: NUMBER converts via getStringValue(double), so I'll test both an integer like 5.0 giving "5" and a non-integer like 5.5 giving "5.5". FALSE, TRUE, NULL, and VOID map to their literal string forms ("false", "true", "null", "undefined"). For NOT, I trace through getPureBooleanValue on the child—NOT(TRUE) resolves since TRUE isn't UNKNOWN, giving "false" after negation, while NOT applied to something that evaluates to UNKNOWN (like NAME "x") breaks and falls through to null. ARRAYLIT uses arrayToString, OBJECTLIT returns "[object Object]", and anything else like an ADD node falls to the default case returning null.

Now I'm covering getArrayElementStringValue: null/undefined nodes give "", EMPTY nodes give "", and everything else delegates to getStringValue. For arrayToString, I check that literals join numeric children with commas, empty literals give "", and if any element resolves to null (like an ADD node), the whole array conversion returns null. Then for getNumberValue, I'm working through TRUE→1.0, FALSE/NULL→0.0, NUMBER(5)→5.0, VOID behaving differently based on side effects (null vs NaN), and NAME nodes like "undefined"/"NaN" giving NaN while "Infinity" gives positive infinity.

I'm continuing with NEG and NOT node handling, confirming unmatched cases fall through to the final `return null;` at the bottom of the switch, then covering how STRING and ARRAYLIT/OBJECTLIT route through getStringValue and getStringNumberValue, with ADD and other defaults returning null. For getStringNumberValue itself, I'm checking edge cases like vertical tab characters forcing null, empty strings trimming to 0.0, valid hex parsing to a number, malformed hex throwing to NaN, and signed hex strings returning null.

Now I'm testing "infinity" variants returning null, normal decimal strings parsing correctly, and malformed strings falling into NaN via exception handling. For whitespace trimming, I'm verifying trimJsWhiteSpace handles plain spaces but treating vertical tab as an uncertain case, and isStrWhiteSpaceChar returning TRUE for space, UNKNOWN for vertical tab, FALSE for regular letters, while being cautious about unicode space-separator categories since their classification isn't fully certain. I'm also starting to look at getFunctionName for cases where a function expression is assigned to a variable name.

For that, I'm constructing a NAME node with a FUNCTION child to represent `var x = function(){}`, then verifying getFunctionName walks up to the parent NAME and returns its qualified name as the string itself. I'm also setting up the ASSIGN case, building a target name node so getFunctionName can pull the qualified name from the assignment's first child.

Then I'm testing the default case where a function declaration sits as a child of a BLOCK, so getFunctionName falls through to reading the function's own first child (its name node) and returning that qualified name, while noting the precondition that the node must actually be a FUNCTION type. Now I'm turning to getNearestFunctionName, checking it returns null for non-function nodes and defers to getFunctionName otherwise.

For the anonymous-function-as-object-literal-value case, I'm tracing through what happens when a function is attached under a STRING_KEY (shorthand object property) - the switch in getFunctionName doesn't have a case for STRING_KEY, so it falls to the default branch, which reads the function's own (empty) name node and returns an empty string rather than null, which could mean getNearestFunctionName never reaches the STRING_KEY fallback branch since empty string isn't null.

I'm wondering whether NAME.getQualifiedName() might actually return null specifically when the name string is empty, which would explain how getFunctionName could produce null for anonymous functions in that default case.

Given the ambiguity, I decide to keep the test simple: I'll focus on the more certain cases like a non-function node returning null and a function with a NAME parent returning the matched name, and skip the uncertain STRING_KEY branch or add a comment noting the assumption.

For isImmutableValue, I'm mapping out the logic - STRING/NUMBER/NULL/TRUE/FALSE all return true, and CAST/NOT/VOID/NEG cases recurse into checking the first child's immutability.

For NAME nodes, only "undefined", "Infinity", and "NaN" return true immutability - anything else falls through and returns false.

Then I move on to checking isSymmetricOperation, isRelationalOperation, and getInverseOperator, which are straightforward token comparisons with defaults, and isLiteralValue, testing cases like CAST of a string literal, ARRAYLIT with empty vs non-literal children, and REGEXP with non-literal contents.

I also work through OBJECTLIT with different STRING_KEY value types, FUNCTION expressions versus declarations under includeFunctions, and the default fallback to isImmutableValue. Then I move into isValidDefineValue, checking STRING/NUMBER/boolean literals directly, ADD expressions where both sides must be valid defines, and starting to consider NOT expressions.

A NAME child in a block should return false, and any non-BLOCK node also returns false for isEmptyBlock. Then I check isSimpleOperatorType against ADD (true) and ASSIGN (false), and start working through mayHaveSideEffects branches, starting with THROW returning true.

Continuing through OBJECTLIT and ARRAYLIT cases: side-effect detection depends on checkForNewObjects flag and whether children contain effects, and I'm setting up VAR nodes with and without children to test empty declarations.

NAME without child gives false with no remaining children to check. For FUNCTION nodes, checkForNewObjects always makes it true; otherwise it depends on whether it's a function expression versus declaration -- an anonymous function expression has no side effects, but a function declaration statement does since it introduces a binding.

For NEW nodes, checkForNewObjects flags it true, but if the constructor itself is known safe (like Array) and checkForNewObjects is false, it falls through to check the children instead. CALL nodes get evaluated by whether the specific function call has side effects (Math.floor doesn't), otherwise falling through to check the arguments. For default cases, simple operators like ADD have no side effects, but assignment operators are checked specially -- assigning to a NAME target returns true directly since it mutates state.

Now tracing through a GETPROP assignment target: since it's not a NAME, it recurses into checkForStateChangeHelper on both target and value, and because GETPROP is itself classified as a simple operator, it falls through to check its own children (the object and property name), which in this case are leaf nodes with no further effects.

With both sides confirmed side-effect free, I move to the isGet branch, unwrapping the assignment target down to the base NAME node. Checking evaluatesToLocalValue on that NAME fails since "a" isn't immutable and there's no local predicate matching it, so I fall through to checking whether the base value is a literal.

Since NAME isn't a literal either, isLiteralValue returns false, meaning !false = true, so mayHaveSideEffects correctly returns true for `a.b = 1;` — assigning to a property of a non-local variable counts as a side effect. Now I want to verify the analogous case where the base is a literal object instead of a variable, testing an assignment like `({}).b = 1;` to see if that comes out differently.

For the final else branch, I need an assignment target that's neither a NAME nor a GET node, which is tricky since valid targets are typically limited. I'll construct an artificial case with ASSIGN(ARRAYLIT(), NUMBER(1)) to force that path, even though it's not a realistic runtime scenario, just to exercise the logic manually.

Tracing through: checkForStateChangeHelper on the empty ARRAYLIT and NUMBER both return false, and since isGet is false we hit the else branch checking isLiteralValue on the target—an empty ARRAYLIT is a literal, so the side effect check returns false overall. I'll note this as a synthetic edge case purely for coverage.

Now moving to constructorCallHasSideEffects—this requires a NEW node and depends on methods like isNoSideEffectsCall and related no-side-effects annotations on Node.

For a NEW node with name "Array" (which is in CONSTRUCTORS_WITHOUT_SIDE_EFFECTS), the function returns false, but for an unknown constructor like "Foo" it returns true, and passing a non-NEW node should throw an IllegalStateException—I'll write tests covering all three cases.

Then for functionCallHasSideEffects, I need a CALL node structure where the callee is a built-in function name like "String" that's in BUILTIN_FUNCTIONS_WITHOUT_SIDEEFFECTS, testing that this correctly reports no side effects.

Now checking callHasLocalResult, which requires an isCall() node and reads the side-effect flags for the FLAG_LOCAL_RESULTS bit — since a default-constructed CALL node has flags of 0, this should return false.

For newHasLocalResult, it checks isOnlyModifiesThisCall() on a NEW node, so I'd expect false for a plain NEW node, and an exception for non-new nodes.

For canBeSideEffected: CALL/NEW nodes always return true; GETPROP/GETELEM always true; a FUNCTION expression returns false; a NAME node returns true unless it's marked constant or found in the known-constants set, in which case false; anything else recurses into children, so something like adding two numbers should return false since neither operand is a CALL or NAME.

For precedence, I'm mapping token types to their numeric precedence values — COMMA is 0, ASSIGN 1, HOOK 2, up through MUL at 12, and CALL grouped with GETELEM/GETPROP at 15 despite documentation suggesting 14. An unrecognized statement-level token like IF should make precedenceWithDefault return -1, and calling precedence() directly on it should throw.

For isUndefined and isNullOrUndefined, VOID nodes and the NAME "undefined" should both return true, while other names or node types return false; NULL should also trigger isNullOrUndefined but not isUndefined. Then I'm checking associativity and commutativity, starting with MUL which should be both associative and commutative.

ADD is neither associative nor commutative in this implementation, while AND is associative but not commutative — I'm verifying these match the code's logic. Next I check isAssignmentOp and getOpFromAssignmentOp by looping through each ASSIGN_* token to confirm the correct base operator is returned, noting that plain ASSIGN passes isAssignmentOp but throws on getOpFromAssignmentOp since it's not handled in the switch; ADD should fail isAssignmentOp entirely. Then isGet should be true for GETPROP/GETELEM and false for NAME, isCallOrNew true for CALL/NEW and false otherwise, and opToStr/opToStrNoFail should map known tokens to strings while an unknown token like NAME returns null from opToStr and throws from opToStrNoFail. Finally I'm testing isLatin, where ordinary ASCII like "abc" passes but a string containing "café" fails since é exceeds the 0x7f threshold.

For isValidSimpleName I test "foo" as valid, "123abc" as invalid since it can't start a valid identifier, "var" as invalid since it's a reserved keyword, and a name containing "ö" as invalid due to failing the Latin check even if it might otherwise be a legal JS identifier — this exercises both the identifier-character and keyword branches. For isValidQualifiedName I check "foo.bar" as valid, while ".foo", "foo.", and "foo..bar" are all invalid because splitting on the dot produces an empty segment that fails isValidSimpleName. Then I move to testing booleanNode for both true and false, producing TRUE/FALSE node types.

I trace numberNode across regular doubles, NaN (which becomes a NAME node), positive infinity (also a NAME node), and negative infinity (a NEG node wrapping the Infinity name), then verify isNaN correctly flags the NaN name node and a zero-divided-by-zero expression as true, while other numeric expressions return false.

Now I'm constructing FOR nodes manually with three versus four children to test isForIn's child-count check, confirming isLoopStructure recognizes FOR/DO/WHILE but not IF, and checking getLoopCodeBlock's differing logic for grabbing the last child on FOR/WHILE versus the first child on DO.

For getConditionExpression I work through the different branches per token type—IF/WHILE grab the first child, DO grabs the last, FOR depends on child count, and other types throw. I also confirm isControlStructure only checks the node's type without touching children, meaning I can safely construct bare nodes for WITH, LABEL, TRY, etc. without worrying about factory validation, which resolves my earlier concern about needing full child structures for those tokens. Then I start setting up a SCRIPT node to test isStatementBlock.

Now I'm verifying isStatement and isStatementParent behavior by building small NAME/BLOCK trees and checking preconditions, confirming isSwitchCase only accepts CASE/DEFAULT_CASE, and isReferenceName only returns true for non-empty NAME nodes. I'm moving into the trickier territory of TRY/CATCH/FINALLY node handling, planning to construct TRY structures manually with try-blocks and catch-container blocks to test hasFinally, getCatchBlock, and related helpers.

Testing maybeAddFinally by starting with a TRY node that has no finally block yet...

Now I'm tracing through removeChild's branching logic: when the parent is a try-finally node and a catch handler exists, removing the finally block just detaches it from the parent, but when there's no catch handler, it instead detaches the finally block's children without removing the block itself.

I'm now checking the isTryCatchNodeContainer branch, verifying that removing catchContainer from tryNode works correctly given the parent-child relationships.

For a plain generic BLOCK node (not try-related), the last fallback just detaches its children directly, since the checks for try-finally, catch, and try-catch-container come first in order.

I'm now tracing other removeChild branches: for a WHILE loop's body BLOCK, node.isBlock() triggers detachChildren, leaving an empty block still attached to the loop. For a statement block or switch-case parent, removeChild simply removes the node from its parent. And for a VAR node with multiple children, removing one child leaves the others intact.

When VAR has exactly one child, removeChild removes that child and then recursively removes the VAR node itself from its own parent block, so I need to nest it inside a BLOCK to trigger that recursive path. Similarly, for a LABEL node whose statement child is being removed, it recursively removes the label from its enclosing block too. I'm also noting that the FOR-loop-with-four-children branch replaces the removed child with an empty node using the source's own IR.empty() call.

For testing the FOR case, I want to build a for-loop with init, condition, increment, and body children, remove the increment child, and confirm it's swapped with an empty node in that position. Then for the invalid case, I want to trigger an IllegalStateException by calling removeChild with a parent/node combination that doesn't match any recognized structural pattern, like using a NUMBER node as the parent with an unrelated child.

Now I'm working through the trickier VAR and LABEL recursive removal cases, which require constructing a grandparent block so the recursive removeChild call has something to operate on. For VAR with a single child, I'm verifying that removing the name node cascades up to remove the whole var statement from its containing block. For LABEL, I'm setting up a similar structure with a block, a label, and a labeled child to test the same recursive removal behavior.

Then I move on to testing tryMergeBlock, checking that a nested block gets merged into its parent block when the parent is a proper statement block, and separately verifying that merging fails when the parent isn't a block (like an IF node).

Next I check isCallOrNewTarget - confirming it returns true only when the node is directly the first child of a CALL/NEW node, false otherwise, and false for standalone nodes with no parent at all.

Then I start testing getArgumentForCallOrNew, verifying it retrieves the correct argument node by index from a call expression's argument list.

I move on to getArgumentForFunction, verifying it retrieves the correct parameter node from a function's parameter list by index.

Now I'm setting up test nodes for prototype property helpers, building a qualified name node representing "Foo.prototype.bar" to test isPrototypeProperty and related functions.

I trace through getPrototypeClassName by walking up from the property node to find the class name portion before ".prototype".

Then I verify getPrototypePropertyName extracts "bar" correctly from the qualified name string, and I set up an EXPR_RESULT with ASSIGN to test isPrototypePropertyDeclaration.

Now I'm building a small test tree with a BLOCK containing a call to "foo" and a sibling NAME "bar", to check functions like containsType, has, and reference-counting utilities.

I'm testing isNameReferenced and getNameReferenceCount by verifying "foo" is detected as referenced while "baz" isn't, then counting occurrences of "bar". I'm also setting up test cases for referencesThis, checking that a function body referencing THIS returns true, but that THIS appearing only inside a nested inner function doesn't count toward the outer function's result since traversal should stop at function boundaries.

Now I'm testing getVarsDeclaredInBranch with a block containing a variable "a" plus a nested function declaring "b" -- expecting only "a" to surface since traversal shouldn't descend into the nested function.
